a.summary: The harness javadoc's claim that the stream's accurate available() is what "lets the JDK gzip reader discover a following concatenated member" describes pre-JDK-25 behaviour; on JDK 25 nothing in the read path ever calls the source stream's available().
a.failure_scenario: Not a test failure: FragmentedInputStream.available() (line 225) is dead weight that the javadoc presents as load-bearing. A maintainer trimming the harness keeps a no-op override, or concludes that concatenated-member coverage is a property of the harness's stream model when it is the JDK's unconditional retry; anyone chasing a future concat regression on this evidence is looking at the wrong lever.

b.summary: The harness javadoc credits accurate `available()` reporting with letting the JDK gzip reader discover a concatenated member, but JDK 25's GZIPInputStream.readTrailer never calls `available()` at all, so the claim is false and the `FragmentedInputStream.available()` override it justifies (line 225) is dead code on every JDK this project targets.
b.failure_scenario: A reader extending this target — e.g. adding a mode that models a real HttpResponseInputStream, or reusing FragmentedInputStream elsewhere — reads line 28 and concludes that accurate `available()` is load-bearing for mode 2's concatenated-gzip round-trip property, and either preserves an override the code under test never calls or, worse, concludes that the round-trip property is an artefact of the model and does not hold for network bodies. Both conclusions are wrong on JDK 25/26: concatenated-member discovery is unconditional there. The README repeats the same framing at sava-rpc/src/test/resources/fuzz/README.md:32.

instructions.question: How does the defect described by `b` relate to the defect described by `a`?
instructions.focus: Compare the defects, not the wording. Two findings about the same code can still be different defects.

criteria: Different defects: fixing the defect `a` describes would leave the defect `b` describes unfixed, even when both sit in the same code.
The same underlying defect, but `b` narrows it, re-scopes which instances or inputs it covers, or reports it at a different place. Not a different defect in adjacent code.
The same defect restated in different words: fixing one fixes the other.

claims_new_evidence.instructions: Does `b` cite evidence that `a` does not?

criteria.true: `b` names a file, test, command, observation, or reproduction that `a` does not mention.
criteria.false: `b` cites nothing beyond what `a` already cites, or cites nothing at all.
